idiom_name: asyncio.timeout / asyncio.wait_for (3.11+) and Future.result(timeout) for threads
implementation_notes: The stdlib dissolves the classic timer into two local idioms: in asyncio, asyncio.timeout(delay) is an async context manager that cancels the current task and surfaces a built-in TimeoutError (the CancelledError is transformed only outside the context manager), asyncio.timeout_at takes an absolute deadline, and asyncio.wait_for cancels the awaitable and raises TimeoutError; for threads, concurrent.futures.Future.result(timeout) together with as_completed/wait timeouts raises TimeoutError without stopping the worker. The context-manager form is what replaces the hand-written timer-and-cancel structure, and it is why the deadline composes with structured concurrency - a TaskGroup propagates the resulting cancellation.
pitfalls: The two meanings of TimeoutError differ: asyncio.timeout/wait_for cancel the awaitable, while concurrent.futures.Future.result(timeout) only stops waiting and leaves the worker thread running.
TimeoutError can only be caught outside the asyncio.timeout block; an inner except sees asyncio.CancelledError and may swallow it.
Cancellation is cooperative: a coroutine inside a blocking call or a CPU loop never reaches the cancel point, so the timeout fires only after it yields back.
Re-arming a fresh asyncio.timeout at every hop resets the budget; use asyncio.timeout_at with one absolute deadline for a request-scoped budget.
